A positive result (a genuine steerable dimensional handle) is equally publishable and directly enables units-aware equation discovery without architectural surgery. 3) Fit and dimensional consistency are partly entangled (the true equation is both well-fitting and consistent); the partial-correlation feature selection and dimension-flipping dissociation pairs (step 5) isolate genuinely fit-independent dimensional signal, and we report where separation is impossible. 4) Some NSR checkpoints do not ingest units at all; we ensure the training data provides per-variable units (Feynman + synthetic) so the model COULD in principle represent dimensions, making the absence claim substantive. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes (which PATCHES shows are partly correlational, so we corroborate with causal patching), and random-direction controls. 6) An internal dimensional probe might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; the interpretability diagnosis (fit-steerable, dimensions-decodable-but-weakly-steerable, type-concept-vs-token-statistics) and the audit/search-pruning payoff remain the contributions, reported honestly. 7) If no blind spot is found (fit steering preserves dimensional consistency), that is a valuable positive result establishing that NSR feature-steering is dimensionally safe and that these models robustly represent physical units.

Name: control_authority_vs_sampling_noise
Title: Signal or Seed Lottery? Whether Interpretable-Feature Steering Actually Controls Scientific Designs or Just Nudges a Distribution Swamped by Sampling Noise
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering of scientific generative models is routinely reported as a mean property shift, but we hypothesize that for a large fraction of features the property VARIANCE induced by ordinary sampling stochasticity (seed/temperature) dwarfs the steering-induced mean shift, so a single steered generation is a seed lottery rather than deterministic control. We further hypothesize an intervention-free 'control-authority' score (steer-shift-to-sampling-spread ratio, estimable from a tiny sample) predicts which steers give reproducible per-object control versus which are effectively noise, and that this reframes when steering can be trusted for real one-shot design.
Related Work: All steering-of-generation work in science reports AGGREGATE mean property shifts: InterPLM (2024), ProtSAE (2025), Steering Protein Language Models/ASPO (2025), CB-pLM (2024), Automated Neuron Labelling (2025), Circuits/Features/Heuristics in Molecular Transformers (2025), Steering Vector Fields for Molecular Generation (2025), and Physics Steering (2025). Crucially, every one of these quantifies success as the average change in a target property across many generations and never separates the steering signal from the sampling-noise floor at the level of an individual design. Text-LLM work on steering-vector unreliability (Understanding the Unreliability of Steering Vectors 2026) studies cross-prompt/method fragility but not the signal-vs-sampling-noise decomposition, and not for scientific objects with objective oracles. The Steering-Vector-Fields paper even notes larger shifts come 'at the expense of validity' but never measures per-generation reproducibility. No prior work (a) decomposes steering-induced mean shift against the sampling-induced property variance to compute a per-feature control-authority ratio, (b) shows that many celebrated steers have authority near or below 1 (seed-lottery regime), or (c) provides a cheap predictor of which steers deliver reproducible one-shot control. This is distinct from my prior blind-spot proposals (which contrast property classes) by asking a stochasticity/reproducibility question about steering ITSELF.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design steers a feature and reports that the target property increased on average. But real design is often one-shot: you generate a design and use it. We ask whether a single steered generation actually delivers the intended property, or whether the property you get is dominated by which random seed you drew. Scientific generative models sample stochastically, so any target property already has a baseline VARIANCE across seeds and temperatures; steering adds a mean SHIFT. We hypothesize that for many interpretable features the shift is small relative to this sampling spread, placing steering in a seed-lottery regime where per-object control is illusory despite a real average effect. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders and exact/cheap property oracles (DSSP/ESMFold, GRAVY, molecular weight; RDKit logP, QED, ring counts), we (1) decompose, per feature, the steering-induced mean shift against the sampling-induced property variance to compute a Control-Authority ratio (Cohen's-d-style shift/spread); (2) establish the seed-lottery phenomenon by measuring the fraction of features whose authority is below a per-object-reliability threshold, and the resulting one-shot success rate; (3) test whether an intervention-free control-authority score estimated from a tiny sample predicts reproducible one-shot control better than the reported mean shift; and (4) show a practical fix—a small best-of-n selection budget guided by an internal property readout—that converts low-authority steers into reliable one-shot designs, tracing an authority-vs-selection-cost frontier. Results recast steering evaluation from mean shifts to per-design reliability.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. PROPERTY oracles (cheap/exact): proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet content (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight; molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic count (RDKit). VALIDITY gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity + SA (molecules). FEATURE BANK: ~30-50 interpretable property-linked features per domain (concept-correlation / probe AUROC) plus difference-of-means directions as a baseline. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + ESMFold on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- for many features the sampling-induced property variance dwarfs the steering-induced mean shift: a single steered draw is a seed lottery): Tests the core decomposition. For each feature/property at a fixed steering strength, generate 200 objects each UNSTEERED and STEERED across many seeds (plus a small temperature sweep). Decisive metric first: CONTROL-AUTHORITY ratio = steering mean shift / unsteered sampling std (a standardized effect size); then per-object OVERLAP = fraction of steered draws that do NOT clear the unsteered distribution's target-property threshold; then ONE-SHOT SUCCESS RATE = probability a single steered draw lands in the target band, contrasted with the AGGREGATE mean shift the steering literature would report (the "works on average vs works once" gap). Matched-norm random-direction control bounds spurious shift. Convincing (H1 holds): a LARGE fraction -- >= 0.3 of bank features -- have control-authority < 1.0 (mean shift below one sampling std) with one-shot success < 0.5, while their aggregate mean shift is nominally "successful", establishing the gap. Undecidable band: seed-lottery fraction in [0.15, 0.3) -> phenomenon present but limited; report the distribution, do not headline. Negative result (< 0.15 of features in the low-authority regime; most have authority >= 1.0 and one-shot success >= 0.5): steering gives reliable per-object control -- a valuable positive result that interpretable steering works one-shot, not just on average.

Experiment 2 (authority-vs-validity frontier -- ruling out that strength trivially buys authority): Supports H1 by showing the seed lottery is not an artifact of one weak strength. Sweep steering strength (6 levels) and, at each, recompute control-authority and validity. Decisive metric first: whether any strength reaches control-authority >= 1.0 at validity retained within 10% of unsteered, traced as an authority-vs-validity frontier. Convincing: for the low-authority features, higher strength raises authority only by driving validity down (no strength achieves authority >= 1.0 at acceptable validity). Undecidable band: a strength reaches authority in [0.8, 1.0) at acceptable validity -> borderline controllable; report the frontier. Negative result: a moderate strength achieves authority >= 1.0 at retained validity -- the seed-lottery framing is strength-specific, reported as such.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- a cheap, intervention-free control-authority score predicts which steers are reliable): Tests the predictor. Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / out-of-sample R^2 of full-sample control-authority (and one-shot success) predicted from a TINY sample (8-16 steered + 8-16 unsteered draws), then precision@k for flagging unreliable steers as a pre-flight check; also test an intervention-free GEOMETRIC predictor (decoder-direction norm relative to residual-stream norm; feature-decoder overlap) and compare both against the reported mean shift and concept-correlation (nested-model comparison). Convincing: the small-sample estimate predicts full-sample authority with |rho| >= 0.6 and precision@10 >= 0.7 for flagging seed-lottery steers, and the geometric predictor adds >= 0.1 R^2 over mean-shift/concept-correlation. Undecidable band: small-sample |rho| in [0.3, 0.5) or precision@10 in [0.5, 0.7) -> a noisy predictor; report the minimal sample size that reaches the band or that none does. Negative result (|rho| < 0.3): authority cannot be predicted cheaply -- the pre-flight-check contribution is withdrawn, leaving the phenomenon (Experiment 1) as the result.

Experiment 4 (payoff -- a selection budget converts seed-lottery steers into reliable control): Tests the practical fix. For low-authority steers apply best-of-n generation ranked by (a) a cheap internal property probe on the steered activation and (b) the external oracle; sweep n. Decisive metric first: one-shot (best-of-n) success rate vs n, traced as an authority-vs-selection-cost frontier -- how many extra samples convert a seed-lottery steer into reliable control, vs high-authority steers that need n=1; then compute cost of internal-probe vs oracle-guided selection. Convincing: best-of-n with internal-probe ranking reaches >= 0.8 success at n <= 8 for low-authority steers, within 2x the compute of oracle-guided selection. Undecidable band: required n in (8, 32] to reach 0.8 -> costly but usable; report the frontier. Negative result (success stays < 0.8 even at n=32, or internal-probe selection no better than random ranking): selection does not rescue low-authority steers cheaply -- reported honestly as a cost the seed lottery imposes.

Experiment 5 (robustness of H1-H2): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, difference-of-means baselines, and >=3 properties per domain, and test whether autoregressive generation shows lower authority (more accumulated noise) than masked-infilling. Report the fraction of cells where the seed-lottery regime and the authority predictor replicate, and the distribution of authority over reasonable target-band widths (the core claim uses the band-agnostic standardized ratio). A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles (ESMFold, DSSP, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal per-design controllability and reproducibility, not experimental function—stated explicitly, though property values are objective given the oracle. 2) Control-authority depends on the chosen target-property band width; we report authority as a distribution over reasonable bands and use a standardized effect-size that is band-agnostic for the core claim. 3) Higher steering strength could raise authority; we sweep strength fully and report the authority-vs-validity frontier so the seed-lottery finding is not an artifact of a single weak strength. 4) The small-sample authority predictor may be noisy; we quantify its calibration and the minimal sample size needed, and compare to intervention-free geometric predictors. 5) The best-of-n fix trades compute for reliability and depends on internal-probe quality; we report the frontier rather than claim a free lunch, and compare internal-probe vs oracle-guided selection. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, difference-of-means baselines, and random-direction controls. 7) If most steers turn out to have high authority (deterministic one-shot control), that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable-feature steering is reliable at the level of individual designs, not just on average.

Name: interpolation_path_validity
Title: Cliffs on the Morphing Path: Do Interpretable-Feature Interpolations Between Two Valid Designs Traverse Valid, Monotone Ground?
Short Hypothesis: When a designer morphs one valid scientific object into another by interpolating in the interpretable SAE feature space of a frozen foundation-model generator, the intermediate designs are NOT reliably valid nor monotone in the property being morphed: the path silently crosses validity 'cliffs' (invalid/unfoldable/unsynthesizable intermediates) and exhibits non-monotone property overshoot, even though both endpoints are valid and the endpoints' property values bracket the intermediates'. We further hypothesize that interpolating in the SAE feature space stays valid and monotone MORE often than interpolating in the raw activation space, and that a cheap intervention-free path-curvature/off-manifold signature predicts where a given interpolation will break.
Related Work: Latent-space interpolation and manifold traversal for design is a mature line: ACAI (2018) regularizes autoencoders for realistic interpolation; STONED (2021), ChemFlow (2024), ChemSpacE (2022), ChemoVerse (2020), and Navigating Chemical Space with Latent Flows all traverse or interpolate WHOLE-OBJECT VAE/GAN latent spaces for molecule discovery; 'Revisiting Latent-Space Interpolation' (2021) benchmarks interpolation ALGORITHMS (linear vs slerp) on VAEs. Crucially, ALL of these (a) operate on bespoke VAE/GAN latent spaces, not the INTERPRETABLE SAE feature space of a frozen foundation-model generator, (b) evaluate interpolation by endpoint recovery, smoothness, or aggregate validity, and (c) never test whether property change along the path is MONOTONE or whether intermediates cross validity CLIFFS, nor tie failures to named interpretable features. SAE-steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, chemistry/RNA SAEs) only does single-point steering and never studies interpolation paths at all. My own prior proposals study endpoint steering, off-mode reach, and side-effect drift, but never the reliability of a design-MORPHING trajectory. This is the first to reframe interpolation-for-lead-optimization as a path-validity/monotonicity reliability question in interpretable feature space, and to contrast SAE-feature vs raw-activation interpolation on that axis.
Abstract: Lead optimization and design exploration routinely proceed by morphing one good design into another—interpolating between two valid objects and picking intermediates. With interpretable sparse autoencoders (SAEs) now decomposing frozen protein and molecule generators into named feature directions, a natural and appealing workflow is to interpolate in this interpretable feature space, reading off which concepts turn on and off along the way. We ask whether that morphing path is trustworthy. Even when both endpoints are valid and their property values bracket the intermediates', the path between them need not stay on the valid manifold or change the property monotonically. We surface a behavioral phenomenon we call path cliffs: interpolations between two valid designs silently cross validity cliffs (invalid, unfoldable, or unsynthesizable intermediates) and exhibit non-monotone property overshoot, a failure invisible to endpoint checks. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with SAEs and cheap oracles (ESMFold pLDDT, RDKit validity/logP, DSSP, GRAVY), we (1) quantify path-validity and monotonicity along interpolations between valid endpoint pairs; (2) test whether SAE-feature-space interpolation stays valid and monotone more often than raw-activation interpolation and simple sequence/graph edits; (3) LOCATE where cliffs occur and which interpretable features flip at the cliff; and (4) validate a cheap intervention-free path-curvature/off-manifold signature that predicts where an interpolation will break, plus a cliff-avoiding reparameterization. Results recast interpretable interpolation from an assumed-smooth design tool into an auditable, geometry-predictable one.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2 AND encode/decode round-trip fidelity verified (object -> activations -> SAE features -> reconstructed activations -> regenerated object recovers the source object within a stated identity/Tanimoto tolerance; paths on SAEs failing round-trip are excluded so cliffs are not round-trip artifacts). PROPERTY/VALIDITY oracles: proteins -- ESMFold pLDDT (validity/foldability), DSSP secondary-structure content, GRAVY, molecular weight, pseudo-perplexity; molecules -- RDKit-validity, logP, QED, ring count, synthetic accessibility. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + ESMFold on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- feature-space interpolation crosses validity cliffs and is non-monotone, despite valid endpoints that bracket the property): Tests the core phenomenon. Data: 500 endpoint PAIRS per domain of VALID objects whose property values bracket a target range (e.g., low-logP and high-logP valid molecules; high-helix and high-sheet valid proteins); encode both to SAE feature space, interpolate along the straight line (and a slerp variant) at K=16 steps, decode each intermediate to an object. Decisive metric first: CLIFF RATE = fraction of paths with >= 1 intermediate that fails validity gates despite valid endpoints; then per-path MONOTONICITY = overshoot/violation score on the morphed property (max deviation outside the endpoint-bracketed range, plus count of step-wise sign reversals); then the BLIND SPOT = predictive power of endpoint validity and endpoint property values for intermediate validity/monotonicity. Convincing: cliff rate >= 0.3 and median monotonicity-violation clearly above a within-object sampling-noise floor, while endpoint features predict intermediate failure at AUROC <= 0.6 (endpoints do not warn of the cliff). Undecidable band: cliff rate in [0.1, 0.3) or endpoint-predictor AUROC in [0.6, 0.7) -> mild/partly-predictable cliffs; report distributions, do not headline. Negative result (cliff rate < 0.1 and monotone within noise): interpolation is reliably valid and monotone -- a valuable positive result establishing feature-space interpolation as a safe design tool.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- SAE-feature interpolation stays valid/monotone MORE often than raw-activation interpolation): Tests the comparative claim. Systems compared, on the SAME endpoint pairs at matched path length: (a) SAE feature-space interpolation, (b) raw residual-activation interpolation (sharing the same decode pathway to isolate the SAE effect), (c) direct object-space interpolation (SMILES edit-path / sequence crossover) as a baseline. Decisive metric first: paired difference in cliff rate (SAE vs raw), then paired difference in monotonicity violation, with random-pair controls and control for endpoint distance. Convincing: SAE cliff rate is lower than raw by an absolute >= 0.1 with a paired test CI excluding 0, and monotonicity is no worse. Undecidable band: paired cliff-rate difference in [0.0, 0.05] -> SAE and raw are equivalent; report parity. Negative result (SAE cliff rate >= raw): SAE interpolation is no safer than raw -- an informative, publishable null about the value of interpretable interpolation, reported honestly.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a cheap intervention-free path-geometry signature predicts cliffs, and a reroute reduces them): Tests the predictor and fix. Predictor: per path, before decoding, compute local off-manifold distance of intermediates (distance to nearest natural-object embedding / SAE reconstruction error) and feature-path curvature (nonlinearity of feature activations along the interpolant). Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / precision@k of the geometry signature for predicting cliff location and monotonicity violation, then, for cliffed paths, whether the drop coincides with abrupt on/off switching of a small feature set (Location) vs smooth blends. Fix: reroute the path to minimize off-manifold distance (small on-manifold projected steps); decisive metric -- reduction in cliff rate and monotonicity violation at MATCHED endpoint fidelity, traced as a cliff-rate-vs-fidelity frontier. Convincing: geometry signature reaches |rho| >= 0.5 / precision@10 >= 0.7 for cliff location, and the reroute cuts cliff rate by >= 30% at fidelity within tolerance. Undecidable band: predictor |rho| in [0.2, 0.4), or reroute cliff reduction in [10%, 30%) -> weak predictor/fix; report the frontier without a strong claim. Negative result (|rho| < 0.2 or reroute reduction < 10%): path geometry does not predict or prevent cliffs -- the predictor/fix contribution is withdrawn, leaving the phenomenon (Experiment 1) as the result.

Experiment 4 (robustness of H1-H3): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, linear vs slerp interpolation, and >=3 properties per domain; report the fraction of cells where cliffs, the SAE-vs-raw advantage, and the geometry predictor replicate, and cliff rate as a function of endpoint distance. Monotonicity claims are restricted to the single property being interpolated toward, with off-target drift reported separately. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles (ESMFold, RDKit, DSSP) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal path reliability of interpretable interpolation, not experimental viability - stated explicitly, though validity/property values are objective given the oracle. 2) SAE encode/decode round-trip is lossy and could itself introduce apparent cliffs; we quantify round-trip fidelity and, as a control, compare against a no-SAE (raw-activation) interpolation that shares the same decode pathway to isolate SAE-specific effects. 3) Cliffs might trivially reflect endpoints being far apart in feature space; we control for path length and report cliff rate as a function of endpoint distance, and use random-endpoint-pair controls. 4) Monotonicity is only meaningful for a chosen morphed property; we restrict monotonicity claims to the single property being interpolated toward and report off-target drift separately. 5) The SAE-beats-raw hypothesis may be property- or model-specific; we test multiple properties, sizes, and SAE variants and report where it fails - a null (SAE no better than raw) is itself an informative, publishable result about the value of interpretable interpolation. 6) The path-geometry predictor may be underpowered; mitigated by many endpoint pairs and both domains. 7) The cliff-avoiding fix may lengthen paths or reduce endpoint fidelity; we quantify the tradeoff on a cliff-rate-vs-fidelity frontier rather than assume a free lunch. 8) If interpolation turns out reliably valid and monotone, that is a valuable positive result establishing interpretable feature-space interpolation as a safe design tool.

Name: antiproperty_design_asymmetry
Title: Design Everything But That: Do Scientific Generators Suffer an Ironic-Rebound Asymmetry Between Positive and Negative Property Specification?
Short Hypothesis: Scientific generative models can causally steer TOWARD a specified structural element (positive design: 'include motif X') but cannot reliably steer to EXCLUDE it while designing everything else freely (negative/anti-property design: 'design a valid object that does NOT contain X'). We hypothesize a positive-vs-negative specification asymmetry: attempting to suppress an element via its interpretable feature triggers an ironic-rebound-like effect—the forbidden element reappears at rates far above the unconditioned base rate—because suppressing a concept requires internally activating it, and a compact 'exclude-X' handle does not exist the way an 'include-X' handle does; an intervention-free rebound signature predicts which anti-property requests will silently fail.
Related Work: Two literatures meet for the first time in scientific design. (1) Text/vision negation interpretability establishes that negation is uniquely hard: 'Strong hallucinations from negation' (2024) proves LMs' string distributions cannot respect logical negation; 'Don't Think of the White Bear' (2025) shows ironic REBOUND—negation instructions paradoxically increase a forbidden concept's accessibility via middle-layer heads that amplify it; INLP (2020) removes a linguistic feature only by null-space PROJECTION (single-vector suppression is insufficient); RePS (2025) and SRS (2025) note suppression is systematically harder and more entangled than positive steering. ALL of this is in text/CLIP with fuzzy concepts. (2) Scientific interpretability-of-generation (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) steers features TOWARD single positive properties and evaluates whether the property appears; none studies negative specification. My own prior intervention_leak proposal asks whether single-feature suppression of a property leaks through alternative DECODING routes; this proposal is different and complementary: it studies the POSITIVE-vs-NEGATIVE SPECIFICATION ASYMMETRY itself—whether 'exclude X while designing everything else' is even a representable, steerable target class, tests the ironic-rebound analog (forbidden element appears ABOVE base rate under suppression), and contrasts it head-to-head against the trivially-easy positive case. This transfers a well-established text/human negation phenomenon into high-stakes scientific design (excluding toxicophores, off-target motifs, disallowed folds), where an anti-property that silently rebounds is a safety failure.
Abstract: Real scientific design constantly specifies what must be ABSENT: a drug candidate must exclude toxicophores, an enzyme must avoid an off-target binding motif, a designed protein must not fold into a disallowed conformation. Yet interpretability-guided design, and the human/text literature it borrows from, has focused almost entirely on POSITIVE specification—steering a feature to ADD a desired element. Negation is known to be uniquely hard for language models: suppressing a concept requires internally activating it, producing ironic rebound where the forbidden concept becomes MORE accessible. We ask whether scientific generative models inherit this, surfacing a phenomenon we call the positive-vs-negative specification asymmetry: models causally steer toward a structural element easily, but attempting to EXCLUDE it while designing everything else freely fails—often making the forbidden element appear ABOVE its unconditioned base rate (a design-space ironic rebound). Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders and hard, exactly-checkable oracles (RDKit SMARTS for toxicophores/functional groups; HMMER/regex for protein motifs; DSSP for disallowed structure), we (1) head-to-head measure positive (include-X) vs negative (exclude-X) specification success at matched steering budget; (2) test the rebound hypothesis—does single-feature suppression push forbidden-element occurrence above base rate?; (3) LOCATE and causally test whether an 'exclude-X' handle exists (does subspace null-projection succeed where single-feature suppression fails?); and (4) AUDIT reliability—does an intervention-free rebound signature (early amplification of the forbidden feature) predict silent anti-property failure? We predict a stark asymmetry, an ironic-rebound analog, and that projection-based exclusion plus a rebound audit partially restore reliable negative design.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. ELEMENT oracles (hard, exact -- presence/absence objective): molecules -- structural-alert-level functional groups / PAINS / common reactive-group SMARTS (RDKit); proteins -- specific motifs (zinc finger, catalytic triad) via HMMER/regex and a disallowed secondary-structure target via DSSP-on-ESMFold. We restrict to structural-alert-level elements with unambiguous detectors and avoid synthesizable-threat detail. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA (molecules), ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins). PRECONDITION: for each element record the UNCONDITIONED base rate (fraction of ordinary generations containing it) over 2,000 samples, so rebound is measured relative to it; select the SAE feature(s) best encoding each element by concept-correlation / probe AUROC. Use ~8-12 elements per domain spanning a range of base rates. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + ESMFold on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 & H2 -- positive inclusion succeeds but negative exclusion fails: the specification asymmetry): Head-to-head test. For each element, at matched steering budget and matched validity, run (a) POSITIVE design -- steer the element's feature to INCLUDE it (measure inclusion success + validity); (b) NEGATIVE design -- steer to EXCLUDE it (negatively clamp the feature) while generating everything else freely (measure EXCLUSION success = fraction of valid generations that do NOT contain the element). Generate 300 objects per condition per element. Decisive metric first: ASYMMETRY GAP = positive success minus negative success at matched budget/validity, across elements and both domains (mixed-effects, effect size, CIs); random-direction and matched-non-element-feature controls. Convincing: mean asymmetry gap >= 0.3 with CI excluding 0, driven by positive success >= 0.6 while negative success is low. Undecidable band: gap in [0.1, 0.3) -> asymmetry present but modest; report, do not headline. Negative result (gap < 0.1; exclusion as easy as inclusion): scientific generators handle anti-property design robustly -- a valuable positive result contrasting with text-LLM negation failures.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- ironic rebound: single-feature suppression pushes the forbidden element ABOVE its base rate): Tests the white-bear effect. Compare forbidden-element occurrence under single-feature SUPPRESSION against the UNCONDITIONED base rate, swept over suppression strength (6 levels). Decisive metric first: REBOUND RATE = fraction of elements whose suppression raises occurrence ABOVE base rate; then rebound magnitude (occurrence minus base rate) and its dependence on suppression strength (does stronger suppression paradoxically increase rebound?); then WHERE it rebounds during autoregressive/iterative generation (whether a small set of components re-amplifies the forbidden feature). Convincing: rebound rate >= 0.3 with rebound magnitude CIs excluding 0, and a positive strength->rebound slope for a majority of rebounding elements. Undecidable band: rebound rate in [0.1, 0.3) or magnitude CI overlapping 0 -> weak/inconsistent rebound; report. Negative result (rebound rate < 0.1; suppression monotonically lowers occurrence): no ironic rebound -- suppression works as intended, reported honestly.

Experiment 3 (H4 -- no compact 'exclude-X' handle exists; reliable negation requires removing a SUBSPACE): Tests the mechanism. Contrast three exclusion mechanisms at matched validity: (a) single-feature negative steering (hypothesized to fail/rebound), (b) SUBSPACE NULL-PROJECTION -- project out the top-k correlated feature directions / SVD subspace (the INLP analog), (c) activation patching from element-free generations. Decisive metric first: exclusion success vs subspace dimension k -- the minimal k that drives occurrence below base rate -- then whether projection succeeds where single-feature suppression fails, then the validity cost at that k. Convincing: single-feature suppression does NOT drive occurrence below base rate at any strength, whereas subspace projection reaches exclusion success >= 0.8 at some k >= 2 with validity retained within 10% -- establishing that negation needs a subspace, not a single 'not' vector. Undecidable band: projection reaches exclusion in [0.5, 0.8) at acceptable validity, or requires k so large validity drops 10-20% -> a costly handle; report the exclusion-vs-validity frontier. Negative result (single-feature suppression alone reaches >= 0.8 exclusion): a compact exclude-X handle DOES exist -- an equally publishable refutation.

Experiment 4 (H5 -- an intervention-free rebound signature predicts which anti-property requests silently fail): Tests the audit payoff. Deploy a REBOUND SIGNATURE read mid-generation (early amplification / coherence of the forbidden element's feature despite active suppression) as an alarm. Systems compared: rebound signature vs output-side signals (validity, pseudo-perplexity, the suppression's apparent forward-pass success). Labels from Experiment 2's eventual forbidden-element presence. Decisive metric first: detection AUROC for eventual forbidden-element presence, then calibration ECE, then compute saved by aborting doomed negative-design requests before full generation + oracle checking. Convincing: signature AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.1 above the best output-side signal, ECE <= 0.1. Undecidable band: signature-minus-output-side AUROC gap in [0.0, 0.05] -> no added value; report parity. Negative result (AUROC < 0.6): no usable rebound signature; the audit payoff is withdrawn, leaving the asymmetry/rebound phenomenon as the contribution.

Experiment 5 (robustness of H1-H5): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, and all elements; report the fraction of cells where the asymmetry, rebound, and subspace-projection fix replicate, and whether rebound is stronger for elements with higher base rate or richer feature redundancy. Report validity/novelty retention throughout. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as element-class-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Element presence/absence is defined by hard, exact oracles (RDKit SMARTS, HMMER/regex, DSSP), a strength that makes the asymmetry and rebound objective; the main proxy is downstream 'harm/function', which we do not claim—claims concern the objectively-checkable structural presence of forbidden elements, and we restrict to structural-alert-level elements with unambiguous detectors, responsibly avoiding synthesizable-threat detail. 2) The 'no exclude-X handle' claim is partly an ABSENCE claim; we mitigate by trying multiple exclusion mechanisms (single-feature negative steering, subspace null-projection, activation patching), sweeping strength, and head-to-head confirming that POSITIVE inclusion succeeds in the same pipeline—so exclusion failure is meaningful, not a weak-model artifact. A positive result (a genuine steerable exclusion handle exists) is equally publishable. 3) Rebound could be confounded with generic off-distribution drift from strong suppression; random-direction and matched-non-element-feature controls, plus measuring occurrence strictly relative to base rate, isolate the rebound-specific effect. 4) Base rates for rare elements may be low, making rebound-above-base-rate easy to trigger trivially; we include elements spanning a range of base rates and report rebound as an effect size relative to base-rate uncertainty. 5) Subspace projection may reduce validity or interpretability; we quantify the exclusion-vs-validity frontier rather than assume a free lunch. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 7) If negative specification turns out as easy as positive (small asymmetry, no rebound), that is a valuable positive result establishing that scientific generators handle anti-property design robustly—unlike text LLMs on linguistic negation.

Name: periodicity_repeat_steering_blindspot
Title: Copy, Don't Just Contain: Do Interpretable Features Control the Periodic Repeat Structure of Generated Proteins, or Only Local Motif Content?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable sparse-autoencoder features of protein language models afford causal, steerable control over LOCAL, single-position content (which residues/motifs appear), but NOT over PERIODIC REPEAT STRUCTURE—the long-range copy-consistency that makes a sequence a genuine tandem-repeat protein (near-identical units repeated at a specified period and count). Consequently, steering a feature to 'make it repetitive' silently produces sequences with repeat-like local content but broken periodicity (wrong unit length, degraded copy-consistency, collapsed foldable repeat topology), a blind spot that local-content and validity checks miss but an exact repeat-detection oracle exposes; and an intervention-free internal periodicity-consistency signal flags it.
Related Work: All protein-LM interpretability/steering work targets LOCAL or single-position properties: InterPLM (2024) and 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs through SAEs' (2025) steer toward local motifs (zinc fingers, transmembrane regions, binding sites); 'Automated Neuron Labelling' (2025) and 'Steering Protein Language Models'/ASPO (2025) steer molecular weight, GRAVY, instability index, secondary-structure content and thermostability; CB-pLM (2024) controls per-position interpretable concepts. Every one evaluates whether a local property/motif appears—none studies PERIODIC REPEAT STRUCTURE, a global, position-coupled property requiring copy-consistency across widely separated positions. Separately, a mature biology literature establishes tandem repeats as ubiquitous (present in ~14% of proteins), functionally important, and exactly detectable with well-established tools (RepeatsDB, CE-Symm, TRIPS; Tandem Repeats in Proteins survey 2015), and difficult even for humans/DNA to synthesize precisely (TReSR 2023). No prior work asks whether the periodic/repeat structure is a causally-steerable design lever, contrasts local-content steerability against periodicity steerability, surfaces the phenomenon that 'repetitive' steering silently breaks periodicity, or provides an internal periodicity audit. This introduces the local-content vs global-periodicity axis into interpretability-of-generation, is distinct from my prior fold/symmetry/epistasis/count proposals (repeats are an exact, countable, copy-consistency invariant, not a fold or an element count), and turns exact repeat detection into a mechanism-and-audit target.
Abstract: Tandem-repeat proteins—sequences built from near-identical units repeated at a regular period—make up roughly 14% of all proteins and underpin scaffolds, binders, and designable modular architectures. Building one requires not just repeat-like local content but long-range COPY-CONSISTENCY: the same unit reproduced faithfully at a specified period and count. Interpretability-guided protein design increasingly steers language-model features to install desired properties, but every demonstrated target is LOCAL (a motif, hydrophobicity, molecular weight). We ask whether interpretable features can causally control periodic repeat structure at all, or only local content. We surface a behavioral phenomenon we call the periodicity blind spot: steering a feature to make a sequence 'repetitive' reliably raises local repeat-like content while failing to enforce the correct period, unit count, and copy-consistency—invisible to composition and validity checks but exposed exactly by repeat-detection tools (T-REKS/HHrepID/CE-Symm on ESMFold structures). Repeats are the ideal testbed because periodicity is an exact, cheap, position-coupled oracle. Using ESM-2 with sparse autoencoders, we (1) LOCATE candidate local-content features and candidate periodicity/copy-consistency features via probing; (2) CAUSALLY test the steerability of each, contrasting content control against periodicity control; (3) INTERPRET whether located periodicity units encode a genuine copy-consistency concept or shallow local-composition proxies; and (4) AUDIT reliability, testing whether an internal periodicity-consistency signal flags silently-broken repeats better than content or model likelihood. We predict content control succeeds, periodicity control is decodable-but-weakly-steerable, and a cheap internal audit catches broken repeats before costly structural validation.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODEL (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins; public checkpoints), generation by masked infilling. Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. PERIODICITY oracles (exact/cheap): sequence-level repeat detection (T-REKS / HHrepID / XSTREAM) returning unit length (PERIOD), copy COUNT, and COPY-CONSISTENCY (mean pairwise identity among detected units); plus a structural repeat check (CE-Symm on ESMFold structures) for foldable repeat topology -- sequence-level oracles lead the core claims, structural repeats corroborate. LOCAL-CONTENT oracles: amino-acid composition, motif/tract presence (regex/HMMER), and a composition-preserving shuffled-sequence control that destroys periodicity (isolating content from structure). VALIDITY gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity. PRECONDITION: confirm the model natively spans a meaningful RANGE of periodicity states (non-repetitive to well-formed repeats); assemble a labeled corpus of repeat vs non-repeat proteins from RepeatsDB (thousands of annotated repeat proteins available; we use ~2,000 repeat + 2,000 non-repeat held-out) plus composition-matched shuffled controls. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + ESMFold + repeat tools on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- local single-position content IS causally steerable): Tests that SAE features steer which residues/motifs appear. Identify LOCAL-CONTENT features (probe AUROC / concept-correlation for composition / motif presence on held-out sequences, retain AUROC >= 0.7). For each of >=8 content features, sweep steering strength (6 levels) during masked infilling, generate 100 sequences per level, and measure the DECISIVE metric first: local-content gain (composition/motif shift) per unit steer, with specificity and a matched-norm random-direction control. Convincing: median content gain per unit steer with Cohen's d >= 0.8 vs random control and monotone dose-response (|rho| >= 0.6) for a majority of features. Undecidable band: d in [0.2, 0.5) or |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) -> content-steerability unestablished for that feature; drop from H2's head-to-head. Negative result (d < 0.2 across features): local content is not steerable, the blind-spot premise collapses; reported as a controllability null.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- NO compact, causally-steerable periodicity/copy-consistency handle): Tests that periodicity is decodable-but-inert. (2a decodability) Probe SAE features and raw activations to predict repeat presence, period, and copy-consistency, controlling for composition via partial correlation AND via composition-matched shuffled controls; decisive metric: periodicity-probe AUROC/R^2 above the composition-matched-shuffle floor. (2b steerability) In the SAME pipeline as Experiment 1, calibrate that content features steer, then attempt to install a specified period/count with high copy-consistency while HOLDING composition fixed, using four interventions (TopK SAE feature, Ordered/Matryoshka feature, difference-of-means repeat-vs-shuffled direction, activation patching from true repeat proteins); also test SET-POINT control -- request specific unit lengths (20, 30, 40) and copy counts and measure exact-target hit-rate vs merely "more repetitive". Decisive metric: periodicity-steering success = fraction of steers installing the intended period/count at copy-consistency above a chosen threshold, with composition held fixed. Convincing support for H2 (a real ABSENCE): periodicity is decodable (2a AUROC >= 0.75 above shuffle floor) yet no intervention reaches > 0.2 set-point success and its effect size is < 1/3 of content steerability (Experiment 1). Undecidable band: 2a AUROC in [0.6, 0.7) above floor (decodability unresolved -- report, do not claim inertness) OR set-point success in [0.2, 0.4) (a weak handle may exist -> claim "weak/partial"). Negative result for H2 (set-point success >= 0.4 for any intervention, effect within 1/3 of content): a genuine periodicity handle EXISTS -- an equally publishable positive enabling modular repeat-protein design; reported as refutation.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- "make it repetitive" steering silently yields repeat-like content but broken periodicity): Tests the core blind spot. For each candidate periodicity feature, sweep steering strength and infill N=100 sequences per level. Decisive metric first: SILENT-BROKEN-REPEAT RATE = fraction of "repetitive-steered", valid sequences with repeat-like composition but FAILING the exact repeat oracle (no detected period / wrong period / copy-consistency below threshold); then blind-spot magnitude = fraction of periodicity-steering displacement landing on the local-content axis rather than the periodicity axis (dose-response); then INVISIBILITY = correlation between composition/validity/pseudo-perplexity and true periodicity, with composition-matched shuffles scoring high on content but zero on periodicity. Random-direction and matched-content-feature controls. Convincing: SILENT-BROKEN-REPEAT RATE >= 0.3 among "repetitive" valid sequences AND invisibility |r| <= 0.2 (standard checks miss broken periodicity). Undecidable band: rate in [0.1, 0.3) or |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> mild blind spot; report magnitude only. Negative result (rate < 0.1 or |r| > 0.4): content steering yields well-formed repeats -- a valuable positive result that PLM feature-steering can control long-range periodic structure.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- an intervention-free internal periodicity-consistency signal flags silently-broken repeats): Tests the audit payoff. Systems compared: internal periodicity-consistency score (periodicity-probe confidence / feature coherence read from the steered activation) vs output-side signals (composition, validity, model likelihood) vs a black-box raw-activation probe. Labels from Experiment 3's oracle. Decisive metric first: detection AUROC for the content-OK/periodicity-broken class, then calibration ECE, then compute saved by flagging non-periodic designs before running CE-Symm/ESMFold structural validation. Convincing: internal AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.1 above the best output-side signal, ECE <= 0.1. Undecidable band: internal-minus-output-side AUROC gap in [0.0, 0.05] -> no added value; report parity. Negative result (internal AUROC < 0.6): no usable internal periodicity signal; the audit payoff is withdrawn, leaving the blind-spot demonstration (Experiment 3) as the contribution.

Experiment 5 (interpretation + robustness of H2-H4): Test whether located "periodicity" units encode a genuine copy-consistency concept (invariant to which residues fill the unit, tracking period/consistency) vs shallow local-composition proxies, using controlled pairs that dissociate periodicity from composition (same composition, repeat vs shuffled; different compositions, same period); auto-label top features via max-activating contexts (do they fire at unit boundaries / on high-identity duplications?). Repeat Experiments 2-4 across two model sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, and short vs long unit lengths / low vs high copy counts; report the fraction of cells where the blind spot and non-steerability replicate and whether periodicity steerability degrades with longer periods and higher copy counts. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Periodicity is measured by well-established repeat-detection tools (T-REKS/HHrepID/CE-Symm), which are near-exact for sequence period/count/copy-consistency and slightly noisier for structural repeats (CE-Symm on predicted structures); we lead with sequence-level oracles for core claims and treat structural repeats as corroborating, reporting oracle sensitivity to thresholds. Claims concern model-internal, oracle-verified periodicity controllability, not wet-lab function—stated explicitly. 2) The periodicity-non-steerability claim is partly an ABSENCE claim; we mitigate by trying multiple intervention types (TopK/Ordered SAE features, difference-of-means, activation patching from real repeat proteins, content-orthogonalized directions), sweeping strength, requiring the model to natively span a periodicity range, and head-to-head calibrating that LOCAL-CONTENT features ARE steerable in the same pipeline—so a null periodicity result is meaningful, not a weak-model artifact. A positive result (a genuine steerable periodicity/copy-consistency handle) is equally publishable and directly enables modular repeat-protein design. 3) Composition and periodicity are partly entangled (repeats bias composition); the partial-correlation feature selection and composition-matched shuffled controls (steps 2,3,5) isolate genuinely composition-independent periodicity signal, and we report where separation is impossible. 4) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes, and random-direction controls. 5) An internal periodicity probe might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; the interpretability diagnosis (content-steerable, periodicity-decodable-but-weakly-steerable) and the audit/compute-saving payoff remain the contributions, reported honestly. 6) Masked-infilling steering of long-range copy-consistency is nontrivial; we standardize on finished-sequence oracle evaluation and use activation patching from true repeats as an architecture-agnostic cross-check. 7) If no blind spot is found (content steering yields well-formed repeats), that is a valuable positive result establishing that PLM feature-steering can control long-range periodic structure.
